it is more the things which he did not say than the things which he did put before us today.
The world situation as revealed by the minister this afternoon, and as one reads about it and watches its kaleidoscopic changes, is certainly one to sober the most frivolous of Canadians. The developments since the summer of 1945 I think can best be described in a general way as a serious deterioration. In many respects the people of the world are abiding in an atmosphere which is somewhat similar in some respects to that which covered the earth in 1938, with the added fear today that stems from the fact that this is the atomic age. Certainly we of this day are groping in confusion and uncertainty; and one is led to ask, where is the brave new world that we were told some years ago we were sacrificing and fighting for during the years from 1939 to 1945, and which was held out to the peoples in the western world to obtain from them an all-out effort against the totalitarian aggressors?
The report of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), after his visit to Europe last autumn, and the speech we heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon have served finally to dispel any illusions at any rate that I might have had that we had even caught hold of the tail of that so-called brave new world.
It is just as well, I think, to take account of some of the things that world war II did to mankind. Nobody won that war. Nobody ever wins a war. Every nation emerged from it materially and physically weakened and, in my judgment, with a considerable decline in the standards of morality and of decency. I suppose that such a result was to be expected as a natural consequence of the training which millions of men from all nations had to be given in the arts of carnage and destruction if they were to win over other millions who were extremely well trained in cruel brutality and complete disregard of human life and suffering. Millions from many nations simply cannot emerge from such training and such activities without some adverse effect upon the general will to resist evil. That, Mr. Speaker, was one of the results or adverse effects that emerged from world war II that I wanted to mention.
Out of that same war, as has already been said, some of the nations emerged all but completely destroyed as great powers. England's vitality was seriously sapped until she could no longer take the initiative in world movements for recovery. Germany was and still is prostrate; France was neutralized, or better, paralysed; Italy had become completely a dependent country. On the other hand

Russia, under the impetus of war and military necessity, discovered sources of new strength and suddenly she became very aggressive. The will to resist her aggression seems to have been dead for two long years and, as a consequence, much of Europe has already fallen to communism. I need only mention Poland, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Roumania, and lately Czechoslovakia, which have become satellite states. It has now become clear to all of us, as the minister so well said this afternoon, that Russia aims at European and Asiatic domination at least, and most likely world domination, for she is convinced that communism and capitalistic enterprise cannot long face each other without armed conflict and without one completely destroying the other.
The picture is by no means complete without mention of the United States and a group of small nations all of which emerged from the war greatly strengthened in some respects, although most of them were materially and physically weakened. The United States demonstrated during the war what free capitalistic enterprise can do in an emergency. Without the immense production from that country and from Britain and Canada, Russia would probably have fallen to Germany's military might. It is now known that most of the time that Russia was receiving help from both Britain and the United States she was plotting her post-war drive for world domination at the end of the war. The initiative or leadership in sponsoring world recovery passed to the United States, and she has become the natural leader of the free democratic nations, at least in the sense that most of the remaining free nations look to her because of her very great industrial power, her very large population, her immense wealth and because of her expressed determination to preserve freedom of enterprise and all the other freedoms.
But our good neighbour to the south also came out of that war ambitious, money-proud, and more materialistic, and with an increase in that spirit of self-interest which was mentioned by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) this afternoon.
Today the world is divided into two camps, each with its mighty champion: Russia in the east, and the United States in the west. How long they can face each other without armed conflict I suppose no one can say. I am not one of those who believe that war is inevitable. I believe that war can be avoided, but I will say, sir, I am convinced that the only way we can avoid a conflict is for the remaining free nations to band themselves together and thus provide a preponderance of united economic, moral and material strength to

prevent further aggression by any totalitarian state or any group of totalitarian states. At the same time I am convinced that we must revitalize and rehabilitate democracy by removing social injustice just as fast as we possibly can and by extending opportunities for our peoples to find for themselves contentment and happiness in real freedom. Only in that way can we demonstrate the superiority of the democratic way of life over the communist way of life.
The world picture is not complete without some mention of another force at work in the societies of the world. The minister did not mention it this afternoon, and I hardly expected him to. I do not believe he is convinced that this force exists, but there are a good many people who are thoroughly convinced that it exists. I am one of those who are convinced of the existence of a group of men, some three or four hundred in number, certainly not less, perhaps more, most of them internationalists and strong advocates of internationalism, who control vast sources of wealth. By means of alliances, interlocking directorates, and machinations of one kind and another they are fast gaining control of the money of the globe.
This is what we in this group have often referred to as world or international finance. It is a tyrannical force just as dangerous and as anti-social as communism. Its tools are imperialism in one form or another, and centralization, which finds its ultimate expression in international cartels. It aims-I speak of international finance-to get control of the economies of the globe. The members of this ring have influence with governments out of all proportion to their numbers, and they are the only beneficiaries of war, which makes it a serious consideration for all mankind.
It seems to me, therefore, that freedom-loving people are faced with two unrighteous forces working for their enslavement-international finance on the one hand, and international communism on the other, the latter proposing to control the people of the globe and to use as its tool the workingman, the proletariat.
The aim of both these forces, international communism and international finance, is power-power over the world. There are many keen students of the whole situation who see behind the scenes co-operation of these two forces. Is it possible that finance and communism, having destroyed the axis powers, having operated quite openly together for a time, and having at last divided the entire world of power into two tremendous conflicting camps, have now reached the parting of the ways? I
wonder. Is it possible that now, facing each other, the one is determined to crush the other, the other to crush the one? I confess Mr. Speaker, I do not know. Certainly there is evidence to support an affirmative answer, and that is one reason why I mention this matter tonight. That is one reason why we must see to it that men and women are put into offices of authority who will get the evidence and give it to the people-conclusive evidence one way or the other.
If we Social Crediters are wrong, for goodness sake come out and show us that we are wrong.
It is easy, very easy.
I am looking, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member who said it is easy to get up on his two feet in this house and show us.
I shall.

A witness of some authority- I could quote any number but I have not the time tonight-has presented evidence. Upton Close in his weekly "Closer Ups" for August 5, 1946, had this to say:
Some of my readers have been unable 'to understand my reference to a new school of big capitalist-communism growing up in America and Britain. It is the same school which, when the time comes, will take us into war with Russia, so that out of the wreckage it can make its group dictators of the round earth.
I do not say that I know the answer, not by any means, but I am convinced that we are in danger from international financial power-hungry men, just as much as we are in danger from international communism. Let us, therefore, not become so preoccupied with the one, international communism, that we fail to prepare our defences and our effective offensive against the other force. I feel that there is danger that we are doing that very thing.
I turn now to another phase of the whole question of international policy, or foreign policy, the question of building a foreign policy for Canada.
As the minister said this afternoon, and said so well, an international policy is a thing of many phases and many aspects. There is defence; there is the question of trade; there is the question of international co-operation, and it even extends into the field of international toleration-all these things. But I say, sir, just briefly, that there are at least two ways of planning any aspect of foreign policy.
In the first place, we might decide what we want and work out a plan of achieving it or
Supply-External Affairs

implementing it, and then announce or publicize it. That is one way. The second way is to announce the plan first and then improvise ways and means of implementing it as you go along.
The United States seems to have followed the latter method, announcing a policy and then improvising means of implementing it as it goes along. What has been the result? Well, it looks to me as though the United States has got herself into a real jam. Not only that, but she has caused the united nation to lose much of what prestige it did have in the world.
In the past few years Canada has, I think, allowed herself to be too much influenced by the policies of the United States of America. Moreover, I think we have been too hasty in committing Canada before the people have been made familiar with what our policy really is. We ought to be much more careful about this in the future. The people of Canada should know where we are headed and, further, they should have a right good idea of the price they will have to pay for the external policies pursued by their government.
I maintain that the people have not been made aware of the price which they will have to pay for the policies to which we have been committed by this government since 1945. In my opinion it is unsafe for us to follow too much the lead of the United States. I say this for various reasons and I will cite just two or three.
In the first place, the United States is a rank amateur in foreign relations. For a good many years the United States refused to take its place in the world community of nations, practising an isolationism in which it was trained in self-interest. And since it is a rank amateur, I would hesitate very much to follow the lead of the United States until she has gained much more experience and has attained much greater stability in international relations.
There is a second reason which I think I have already mentioned, international finance. With the outbreak of world war II, Wall Street suddenly became the headquarters of practically the whole ring of international financiers. That is their headquarters today. I do not cast suspicion on the United States of America when I say what I am saying. I have great respect for our neighbours to the south. I have great love and respect for those people. My own parents came from the United States of America. But when I speak of Wall Street as being the headquarters of the international gang who are plotting, I believe, without any question in my mind, to

control the finances of the world, I say we must keep our eye on Wall Street. The very fact that international finance has its headquarters in New York would lead almost any student to suspect that the men who control the international exchanges would attempt unduly to influence the government of the country in which they live. I say we should either confirm or remove completely the suspicion that Wall Street is today the head of this international gang.
How?
I say that we must keep our eye on Wall Street.
How are we to do that?

The third reason why I would hesitate to follow the United States in formulating external policies is this. I have been reading lately of the revelations concerning the agreements at Yalta and Teheran. I do not like to speak disrespectfully of any man who has stood at the head of a nation, but I am prepared to say that the United States made a deal with Russia at Yalta which resulted in the crucifixion of a great country, Poland.
Hear, hear.
Explain.
The hon. member would not understand even if I explained.
Hear, hear. That is right.

All the facts concerning the agreements which were made at Yalta and Teheran are just now coming to light. Poland and its crucifixion must now be looked upon as the gift which the United States was prepared to give in order to pacify the very power that is today attempting to cut the throats of United States, Canada-
The hon. member would have done better than Roosevelt, would he?
-and of every other free nation.

I should now just like to say a few words about my experience at the united nations assembly. I was deeply grateful for the opportunity of going to Lake Success. I personally complimented the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the adoption of the new policy which made it possible for members of opposition parties to go to the united nations assembly as advisers, free to speak their minds there, here or elsewhere.
Did they take your advice?
I took their advice.
I asked, did they take your advice?
No, I am afraid not.
Fortunately they did not.

I will attempt to show that it was not so fortunate, as events have turned out. As I say, I was grateful for that opportunity. I tried to do my best while I was there. For nearly a month I attended practically every session, and I was deeply interested in watching this moving drama on the world stage. It was interesting. Sometimes I found it most depressing. I watched the work for a month, and I saw there what made me feel depressed, namely a display of extremely ill-temper. I noted, sir, a serious decline in manners and in humour. As a matter of fact, I did not see much display of that commodity in the whole time I was there. I noted particularly that day after day, in some of these committee debates or discussions, free discussion amongst men degenerated into debate by-what shall I say? These people certainly departed from logic and reason, and it seemed to me that they entered into debate by studied insult. I was happy to note, however, that the democratic nations used great restraint and patience. Our representatives followed that course. I want to compliment them on the way in which they conducted themselves in that regard. Insult and the departure in debate from logic and reason were the means followed by the totalitarian states, led by Russia. Vishinsky, Gromyko, Doctor Bebler of Yugoslavia and others used that style, and they were the only ones who did so; it was somewhat depressing. But it was a measure of great satisfaction to me to note, as I say, the patience, good judgment and restraint used by the democratic nations.
I saw the assembly used by the satellites of Russia as a propaganda body. That was one reason why I believe Russia was anxious to see the headquarters of the united nations established in the United States. I could not escape the feeling that Russia supported the idea of having the united nations headquarters in the United States and the sessions of the last assembly held1 at Lake Success, because they knew that there was a free press there which was willing and anxious to publicize every single thing these fellows had to say-
That is right.

-that they had freedom of speech and could say anything they liked, which was something they could not do in their own country. The people of the United States, big-hearted as they are, were naive enough to play up Vishinsky, Gromyko and these others, putting what they said in headlines in the biggest type they could' get and spreading that over the country far and wide, with every radio blaring forth the full measure of this propaganda. I recall that, after Vishinsky made his first vituperative speech, one of the Russian delegates told us at a reception that Vishinsky received thousands of telegrams, letters and cables from people in the United States complimenting him on the stand he took when he called certain people-he named a good many people in the United States, put the spotlight on them-warmongers. The Russians knew what they were doing when they supported the establishment of the headquarters of the united nations assembly in New York. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it would have been the smartest possible move for the nations of the world to have established the headquarters of the united nations as near as they could get it to the Russian boundary.
They would not have the free press.
Why?
Send him to school.

Yes. I think we had better send him to school.
At times, Mr. Speaker, as I witnessed the interplay of those forces at the united nations, I was led to feel just what Doctor Evatt of Australia so well expressed when he said, "There is a danger that the united nations is becoming all harness and no horse". However I did see a useful purpose. The assembly was certainly a sounding-board for world opinion, if it were used for that purpose; but all too frequently it was used for airing purely national politics, or for propaganda.
While I was there I attended most of the sessions of the Palestine committee, and I should like to say just a few words about the Palestine situation. I hope I may be able to deal with it objectively and fairly, because
Supply-External Affairs

certainly I am not a partisan with respect to any of the parties concerned in the affairs of that most unfortunate country. I thought it was a marvellous debate. For the first time in history, as far as I know, the best debaters on that subject in the world met together in a body where they were unfettered, where they were free to speak without fear of unfair criticism or the smear that is all too often used in such cases when men differ one with another. I believe practically all the facts concerning that whole problem were brought before the world in those debates. After listening to the debates for about a month, up to what I thought was the rather weak declaration made by Mr. Herschel Johnson, when he declared the position of the United States after stalling for weeks to work up enough courage to do so, I came to the conclusion that the advocates of partition had failed to make out a case sufficiently strong to warrant a recommendation going to the security council for partition. I thought by far the stronger case was made by those who opposed it; and I am not speaking now of the Arabs alone. I refer to the delegates from India, from China and from several other countries whose contributions I thought were outstanding.
Well, eventually, after following all that was said, I concluded it would be wise for me to advise the delegation that I thought they should not vote for partition. I did so, and I believe I was right. It was not because I felt the Jews should not have a national home. No. I believe with all my heart that the Jewish people are entitled to a place where they can live their lives and develop their culture as they desire. I have never deviated from that belief for the last twenty years. But I thought partition was not the answer at this time.
Why?

The Canadian delegation say they voted for the lesser of two evils. I am afraid I must contend that they were unduly influenced by the United States, and by the fact that the report of the Palestine committee was very largely the work of an eminent Canadian, Mr. Justice Rand. So I suppose it is only natural that they should say, "Well, what other course could we have taken?"
To answer that question I shall need just a few moments. It seems to me it must have been obvious to anyone who studied the whole history of Palestine that promises had been made to both Arabs and Jews in years past and at various times, which made it impossible to partition Palestine without doing grave injustice to one side or the other. In 1915

General MacMahon, in the name of the British government, did make a pledge to the Arabs in a bid for their support in the war against the Turks. In 1917, it is true, the Balfour declaration by Great Britain promised the Jews a national home and lifted the hopes of the Jewish people that in due course they would be able to return to that land, develop their own culture and live at peace. But I ask any fair-minded man: How in the world could the Balfour declaration be implemented if the promise to the Arabs were implemented also? Obviously it was an impossibility; and that being the case, a national home for the Jewish people could not be set up in Palestine without doing injustice to the Arab people.
A greater statesman than Balfour!

There was another point. Very early in the game the Canadian delegation could have taken this stand: "We do not think the time is ripe to establish a Jewish national state. Some time it may be, but what is the rush? We feel that the wisest course would be to establish what is right and just and righteous, and then try to find means of working it out."
Then it seems to me that Canada was neglectful of her duty some years ago when, at the height of Britain's troubles in administering the affairs of Palestine, the United States entered into what was to it the ancient and honourable game of "twisting the lion's tail." Almost immediately after the first great war, after Britain was given the mandate over Palestine, criticism began to emanate from the United States, aimed at undermining Britain and making it difficult for her to do the job. That continued and increased in force and frequency as the years went by, particularly after the issuance of the white paper in 1939, which for a time abrogated the Balfour declaration, and temporarily put a stop to the immigration of Jewish people into Palestine. Almost immediately thereafter, while Britain's hands were full, conducting a great war, that criticism continued. Terrorism started, and it was not confined to one side. In some respects the Arabs were just as guilty as the Jews in this regard. Terrorism and aggression and force were used. But in the United States high officials, including even the President, criticized; and their criticism of Britain was anything but fair and just under the circumstances.
It seems to me that this is what Canada should have done at that time. Canada should have stepped forward and stood

Supply-External Affairs
shoulder to shoulder with Britain, declaring to the world that she would help Britain resist the attempt to undermine her. We failed Britain then.

speechtext: I would call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that his time has expired.
May I have another moment or two?
Go on.

Canada should have declared to the world that so long as Great Britain was trying her best to exercise the mandate, and to discharge her responsibilities under it, Canada would stand beside her. We said nothing.

Hear,
hear.

Our silence may have been interpreted in various ways. It may have been interpreted

not by my hon. friend, of course, who keeps on interrupting; he could not interpret anything.
You will find that out later.

It might have been interpreted as a tacit agreement on the part of Canada that the criticism of the United States was correct. At any rate Great Britain's prestige was weakened. The criticism coming from the United States encouraged lawlessness in Palestine, and undermined the authority of the mandatory power.
It seems to me that Canada at the united nations could have taken this position, and I so advocated. One of the major complicating factors in the whole Palestine problem was the refugee situation in Europe. I think Canada should have declared that the Palestine problem could have been reduced to much more manageable proportions had the first step been to strengthen the work of the international refugee organization to the point where that refugee problem was first solved.
The approximately one million people within the refugee camps in Europe should have been taken care of. China said-and may I say I was much touched by the attitude China displayed-"For many years we have had in the midst of China a thriving Jewish community that has been free to develop its culture as it wished, without molestation from us. They have contributed much to that community. We have given refuge to a great many Jews who were persecuted at the beginning of the Hitlerian regime. We are prepared
to take our share of those people in the refugee camps; and we call upon all nations to declare themselves likewise."
There was too much tendency in the propaganda emanating from various sources in the world to treat the refugee problem as an exclusively Jewish problem. The refugee problem was not an exclusively Jewish problem, because there were only about 200,000 Jews in those internment camps. The remainder were Europeans of various nationalities.
I say that if the united nations assembly had first tackled that problem it would have made it possible to reduce the pressure on the Palestine problem to a point where I believe it could have been managed much more efficiently than it was. And surely that great human problem of the refugees-a million of them, languishing behind the fences of those camps-is a sore blot on the humanitarian feelings and aspects of the various peoples of the nations of the world. Until such time as those people are given a home, and until Canada takes her share, and until the United States takes her share, I am afraid we shall not be able to lift our heads without shame.
India declared that she would take her share of them. I am going to close with this thought-

Hear,
hear.
-that Great Britain could have been prevailed upon to remain in Palestine.
Do not coax her.

I should say not now. But I am sure that Great Britain could have been prevailed -upon to remain, had she felt that she had the support of the western powers in the discharge of the onerous duties of -her mandate. I am satisfied she would not have announced her early withdrawal. I think Canada should have supported her. I think Canada should have called for united action in suppressing terrorism and acts of violence in Palestine, and in asking Great Britain to remain there for a period of years, and to have assured her united assistance in the discharge of her duties. And finally, at the end of a few years of 'peaceful living in that unhappy land, the logical thing to do, if we were to abide by the spirit of the united nations charter, as expressed in the preamble, would have been to extend to the people of Palestine the right of self-determination.
If that had been done I believe it would not have been long until the faith of those who believed in the return of the Jews to Palestine could have been justified. Where was the faith, let us say, of the Jews? Where was the

faith that they had when, with Moses, they looked upon the supposedly uncrossable waters of the Red sea? Did they have a Stern gang then? Did they have an Irgun Zvai Leumi?
We waited two thousand years and it did not work out.
I agree, and I sympathize very much with the hon. member.
Do you? Don't send me flowers.

I sympathize much with the hon. member; but nothing can justify the use of force and terrorism. And I am going to say, in conclusion, that the Jewish people and the Arab people, both of them, lose the sympathy of the western nations through their terrorism and their acts of violence.
A Gallup poll was conducted in Canada on February 7, 1948-
Keep your sympathy and give us Palestine.
Might I be permitted to quote this one reference?
Go ahead.
Proceed.

This question was asked in the poll taken in February 1948: when you hear on the radio anything about the dispute between the Arabs and the Jews in Palestine, do you find yourself sympathizing more with one side than the other? The replies showed that 58 per cent had no particular sympathies; 23 per cent had sympathies with the Arabs, and 19 per cent with the Jews. Why? Western peoples do not condone acts of violence.
The welfare of the Jews is bound up with the western powers, not with the eastern powers. The western powers have been their friends; Great Britain has been the greatest friend the Jews have ever had; and it should be their faith that, given time and support, Great Britain would do full justice to and by them.
Mr. Smith from the United States would be very proud of you.

Mr. Speaker, I have never attended any meeting at Lake Success; but, listening to the two last speakers, I had the impression of attending a meeting of the united nations.
I listened with pencil in hand to the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the C.C.F. 
Afterwards I had to put my notes in order. But unfortunately I could not listen with pencil in hand when the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) was speaking. In the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar there are some rays of hope, because he said this: "Even in these disturbing times there is no reason why war should be imminent or inevitable." This I like. I find it comforting, and an oasis of hope in a desert of distress.
He spoke also of close economic co-operation, which was not to be regarded as a military alliance for war. This is evident, provided that the economic co-operation is not so close as to strangle one. In the third place, he mentioned an attempt at democratic reconstruction to establish a strong democratic political force. This is a fine phrase; I do not know exactly what it means, but it sounds quite good. In all that he said there was not a single word of praise for the united nations. I listened to the leader of the Social Credit party and there was not one word of praise for the united nations. I hope I am not misquoting anyone when I say that.
Unfortunately I had to leave during the able speech of the minister of external affairs. All that he mentioned that was good was the establishment of three new states in the British empire or commonwealth; Ceylon, Pakistan and India. That was all. What did the C.C.F. leader praise about the accomplishments of the united nations in three years? Nothing. What did the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) praise? I do not know. I do not assume that he went any farther because, when I came back to the chamber, he looked very sad about the accomplishments of the united nations. For three years we have had discussions about the united nations. Everybody went to San Francisco; everybody went all over the world, and there were delegations of members of parliament who went to see the wise men and decide the future of the world. Nothing good has been accomplished apparently because no praise has been given.
The same thing happened in connection with the imperial conferences of 1926, 1930, et cetera. The leader of the C.C.F. group made wishes. It is most extraordinary that at the imperial conferences before and after 1930 all that was done by the delegates was to express wishes. They met together and they made wishes. The C.C.F. leader made wishes about the control of atomic energy and the defence of freedom and democracy everywhere.
That is a nice phrase; it sounds good but it means nothing. He spoke of fundamental

human rights. I was bom with the idea that the man who lives within the law has certain rights. Apparently the hon. member is for the defence of fundamental human rights. What are those rights? He did not enumerate them. It is not in Canada that we are deprived of human rights to any large extent that we have to form a union of all the nations in order to protect our fundamental rights. It is in the larger nations like Russia and its satellites where these rights are affected.
How are we to go about having these rights respected in Russia? There are two ways we can do so. First, we can discuss it with Russia or, second, we can go to war with Russia and impose our way of life on Russia just the same as General MacArthur is imposing it on Japan which is ready to accept that point of view. He is making himself the defender of such actions. I ask the hon. gentleman if this can be done by means other than conciliation, discussion and compromise, on the one hand, or on the other, by the use of weapons, the going to war in order to humiliate a country and to impose our will on it?
We have an example in Japan. Shall we go to war with Russia? We must be logical. If we are to impose these ideas on a country which denies them, the only thing to do is to go to war with that country. The hon. gentleman-when I say "hon. gentleman" I refer to the leader of the C.C.F. group-said that Russia and the United States had emerged from the war as the giants of our time. That is quite true. But that leaves the British empire behind. The two giants are Russia and the United States; the British empire is behind. The hon. member did not say that, but when he referred to two giants he did not mean three.
Then he complained of the division of spheres of influence at Teheran, Yalta and Potsdam. He was not as precise and definite as the leader of the Social Credit group, but he complained of the secret treaties entered into by the three big powers, the United States, Russia and Great Britain at those three places. President Roosevelt attended the first two conferences while President Truman attended the other.
Then he said that the great powers have set aside the agreements which were made during the war. There were two kinds of agreements made by the big powers, the public agreements which were not respected and the secret agreements which were respected. The secret agreements entered into at Teheran, Yalta and Potsdam were put into force while the Atlantic charter was set aside.
He said that we had condoned the annexation of the Baltic republics, and of Poland. What about the Balkans? If I am not mistaken the minister spoke of the Balkans and of Czechoslovakia. But this is continuing to blame the united nations, although he said that everything that had been done by the united nations was not to be praised.
He concluded rather illogically by sponsoring the relinquishment of an out-moded-national sovereignty. He is a citizen of the world, and he thinks that national sovereignty is out-moded, that the abandonment of our national sovereignty will bring us a premium in the way of an extension of our powers into the affairs of the world at large. Our reward for abandoning our sovereignty will be that we shall have a wider scope in interesting ourselves in the affairs of other countries, and perhaps we shall do just as well as the great powers have done. However, we have no policy.
There is no difference between Ukrainia and Canada except that Ukrainia is under Moscow and Canada is under London. It is the same thing except that they are on opposite sides. We beat the drum .and continue under the illusion that we are running the world. I am sad about it. We should have more of a sense of reality, more of a sense of proportion and a little more imagination.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed for many years the question of foreign affairs. I did so long
before I became a member of this house, and I am surprised that more interest has not been taken in this department of government, since it affects the life, liberty and security of every citizen of the country. With so many universities in the country, there are too many pacifist professors and other people who fail to understand that in days like these might plus right is right.
We are living in the midst of a very dangerous situation. I referred to this the other night, when I asked the question that I am about to put to the house once more: from whom did we derive the freedom and liberty which not only we in this country, but the people throughout the North American continent have enjoyed for the past hundred years? Anyone who is sufficiently fair-minded and who will read attentively the lessons of history, including what great English, American and French historians have had to say, will admit, I believe, that the liberty of which we boast today is a possession which we owe to the mother country. Had not the mother country been mistress of the seas for four centuries, maintaining our liberties against Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon and against dictators in world wars twice in our own time, the liberty that we enjoy today would not have been ours.
That agency alone, the supremacy of the motherland on the seas, has protected America's shores. We remember the Holy Alliance on the part of Prussia, Austria and Russia under Alexander the Great, which lasted for eight years, from 1815 to 1823, and we know that Canning studied carefully the situation in Europe, with the result that the United States promulgated what was known as the Monroe Doctrine. What was the Monroe Doctrine in reality, from the year 1815 to the outbreak of the Spanish-American war in 1898? In reality it meant the protection which America, including our country, enjoyed through the supremacy of Britain on the seas. That was the Monroe Doctrine to 1917.
Had it not been for British naval supremacy, we would have been invaded long ago. In 1938 I was almost the only member in the House of Commons who consistently drew attention to the situation that confronted the people of this country. I pointed out that we had no fleet, army or air force at all. A return was brought down in the House of Commons showing that we had a few boats only; the total tonnage was about that of one large 10,000-ton freighter, and there were three or four ships that really could not go to sea. Today we are facing very dangerous conditions. There is the drastic curtailment of the British empire, civil war in India, revolution in France, race war in Palestine, some kind of struggle between Soviet Russia and the United States, and various other strifes, too numerous to mention, in other corners of the world.
There is no such thing as "Peace on earth, good will toward men". The other day there was a meeting in England at which the Earl of Athlone presided. The Archbishop of Canterbury was there, as was the Cardinal of Westminster, who visited this building last summer. There -were also the moderator of the Presbyterian church, and representatives of the Free Church of Scotland, the Baptist church and others. What did they declare for? They declared that Christianity is facing a very difficult struggle, and said that if we are to have peace on earth and good will toward men, and if we are to have the gospel of Christianity, from now on Christian churches must stand together against communism or communism will win. That was what was said.
Last Monday, after the king and queen had celebrated their anniversary, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Doctor Geoffrey Fisher, denounced communism as a-
. . . militant political S3rstem which in denying God, degrades and enslaves men.
That system reveals itself in its working as utterly hostile to the basic principles of Christianity and of human liberty.

Because of its totalitarian claims it must be resisted at every point; but the final answer can only be given by a free society which so expresses freedom as to abolish the social and economic disorders out of which communism sprang.
I should like to quote what a great bishop of the Church of England, the gifted and learned Right Reverend R. J. Renison, said, in part, in an article yesterday in the Globe and Mail editorial page on "Where are the Peacemakers?"
Where are the Peacemakers?
The Kingdom of Jesus is a Kingdom of Peace. That was one of the names given to Him by ancient prophecy-"The Prince of Peace." That was the hymn the angels sang on the night of His lowly birth. "Peace on Earth." That was the picture given to us by prophet and psalmist of the reign of Christ. It is a reign of love and brotherhood and peace.
And again:
If we were living in a Christian world, there would be no war. The first thing to remember is that you cannot separate human life as a whole from the question of war. We have no faith in the argument as to what the attitude of Christ would be in the world today based on Bible texts, flung from one side or the other. We must remember that Christianity is a spiritual thing that grows from the inside, and we must accept the present crisis in terms of challenge rather than dismay.
And again:
"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God." In the original Greek they are called the sons of God.
The united nations at Lake Success do not mention any of that in their charter. The mother country is one of the greatest nations that we have ever seen in the world. As Tennyson said in his "In Memoriam":
Our little systems have their day;
They have their day and cease to be.
They are but broken lights of Thee,
And Thou, O Lord, art more than they.
As James Thomson said in his poem "The
Seasons":
The nations not so blessed as Thee Must in their turn to tyrants fall Whilst thou shall flourish Shall flourish great and free The dread and envy of them all.
Britain will not sit back and be content to be a second-class power. She still rules the waves. As James Thomson, the Scotch poet, said when he wrote "Rule Britannia", Britons never shall be slaves.
Next to the Christian church, no other agency has done so much for the freedom of the world, and for civilization as has the mother country on the seven seas. The mother country, notwithstanding the terms of the Bretton Woods agreement and the hard terms of the United States loan, can live a few more months the hard way. We have seen [DOT]ecently the collapse of statesmanship.
Sir John Macdonald laid down the policy of this party back in 1844 when he said that the prosperity of Canada depended upon its permanent connection with the mother country and that he would resist to the utmost any attempt, from whatever quarter it might come, which would tend to weaken that union. He went on to say:
For a century and a half this country lias grown and flourished under the protecting aegis of the British crown. Under the broad folds of the Union Jack, we enjoy the most ample liberty, we govern ourselves as we please, and at the same time we participate in the advantages which flow from association with the mightiest empire the world has ever seen. As for myself, my course is clear. A British subject I was born and a British subject I will die.
That has been the consistent policy of the Laurier government. As Sir Wilfrid said, when Great Britain is at war, Canada is also at war. Sir Wilfrid went over to the diamond jubilee celebration and he was the first in the diamond jubilee procession. He established British preferential trade for which he deserves a great deal of credit. He was a beloved figure in this country.
I realize that economics are partly to blame for war, but in this connection I should like to quote the first verse of chapter four of the general epistle of James, which reads:
From whence come wars -and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
That is correct. We have something like that here in connection with the bases on the Atlantic from Newfoundland to British Guiana. These were given under 99-year leases during the war. I contend that those leases should be cancelled and charged to lend-Iease. I realize that, had they not been there in the battle of the Atlantic, the shores of North America would have been invaded.
There will be another opportunity to speak. I have great respect for the minister, and I am sorry the government of the day and the opposition have not some other policy to depend on than the united nations at Lake Success because they are going to find out in a few days, as the historians will record, that it is of no great value as an agency for the peace of the world and security and will not make it any easier for the United States to get on with Soviet Russia.

Mr. Speaker, I will preface my remarks by felicitating most sincerely the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) upon the wonderful peroration he made this afternoon, which no doubt will be a guide and a chart to the Canadian people generally speaking

I am not in entire agreement with some of the statements that have been made, although no one can doubt their sincerity. I should like to make one or two brief references to parts of the fine speech delivered by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He knows that I have great respect for him. I appreciate the talents he has given so freely to the House of Commons. He is really an asset here.
There are some things which I believe could easily have been left out of a discussion of this kind. In referring to the rehabilitation of Europe, he said that he did not think capitalism should be revived. I cannot understand why an expression like that is being used in such a discussion. We know that the word "capitalism" in itself does not mean anything. What we have in this country and what we have in most sections of the world is progressive capitalism. Almost in the same breath, a few moments afterward, he found it possible, and rightly so, highly to compliment the United States and Canada upon the help which they intend to give under ERP.
The United States is a progressive capitalistic country. The same is true of Canada, and that would apply also to South America and many others that I have no time to mention. I cannot comprehend why he should find it possible to criticize the system we have in this country, the system with which the majority of people seem to be in agreement. I would rather have progressive capitalism than governmental capitalism such as they have in Russia. We must of necessity remember these things when discussing a matter of this kind.
I would be the last person to criticize the leader of the C.C.F., but I do not think he should have tried to tie in fascism with the capitalistic right. What has the capitalistic right to do with fascism? Is there any fascism in this country? I repeat that the great majority of the Canadian people believe implicitly in progressive capitalism. I for one believe in it. Practically all the people in Canada believe in that system. That is why I deplore to a certain extent that the hon. member, in his masterpiece of a speech, should have tried to slap the face of progressive capitalism upon which the countries of western Europe and Asia, all the devastated nations, must of necessity rely at the present time to receive the help they require. Help will be given liberally, but it will be from so-called progressive capitalistic systems.
Let us visualize for a moment what happened during the last war. Was not Great

Britain, that fine, heroic nation, operating under the*progressive capitalistic system? Was not Canada a progressive capitalistic country? We know that the United States, the country which came along with us later, is also a progressive capitalistic country. What did we do under that system? By our inventiveness, our terrific and almost unlimited products we pulverized fascism and nazism, and were in a position to help an ally which had governmental capitalism. That should be appreciated; that should be considered.
I have no quarrel with any parties in this country or with their political ideologies, outside of communism, but why try to put progressive capitalism on the same level as fascism or communism? Such a statement is absolutely unfair and unwarranted. Why condemn a system which has proven satisfactory and beneficial, not only to our cause and that of our allies but to the whole of Europe and the world, and which will be able to do still more?
I speak with all humility on external affairs. The united nations and its activities have been severely criticized by the two previous speakers, but if we would be fair we should reflect how hard it is for us to settle our own national and even regional problems in Canada. We have spent the greater part of the last three weeks, for instance, in discussing freight rates, which no doubt is a national problem, and that discussion should have made us realize how difficult it is in a country like Canada, where we enjoy to the full democracy and freedom of speech, to find a solution of our national or even regional problems. If in a country like Canada, which is blessed with prosperity and where our people live together in harmony, it is difficult for our governments, dominion, provincial and municipal, to solve their problems, how much more difficult it must be for the united nations, with fifty-seven members, coming from every section of the world, to find solutions for complex international problems. It is easy to say: what audacity you members of the Canadian parliament have to try to solve the problems of the world by a wave of the hand, by propounding certain ideas you have at heart, when you cannot solve the problems in your own country. But unless we practise unity of purpose and try to reach a common understanding of each other's problems, how can we expect the fifty-seven nations who are members of the united nations to have unity and co-operation and that much-needed understanding in a so much wider field of action.
Unlike the two previous speakers, I do not believe that the united nations is a pipe

dream. It is a living reality that has already accomplished great things. Let us visualize for a moment the alternative if we did not have the united nations at the present time. What would have happened in Greece, Indonesia, China and other danger points in the world? Perhaps our hopes were too high when the nations of the world met in San Francisco, but there was reason for exaltation at that time when the nations of the world got together with the war still raging, with Japan not then defeated, and so that meeting was received with great enthusiasm and high hopes which led to the formulating of the charter, a marvellous document which, if we would implement it in spirit and accept its worthy principles, would help to bring peace and unity to this world.
It would be presumptuous of me to say that the united nations has not difficult problems before it; that it always functioned smoothly, but I know that the Canadian people are fair on that score. In my own constituency I happen to be very fortunate. We have at least a dozen study groups which, over the past few years, have held several meetings to discuss the activities of the united nations, external affairs and international problems. They have set to work to study these problems seriously and have received the necessary information from the personnel of the united nations. On several occasions I was asked to speak to them. The result has been that they are realists and they know and fully appreciate what has already been accomplished by the united nations.
It would be unfair for me to say we are absolutely satisfied with all the activities of the united nations. Some of the criticisms levelled against it by previous speakers are no doubt warranted and necessary to make; but I repeat, let us be realists and face the fact that our own problems in this country, the grain question, maritime rights, the flood situation, freight rates-I could go on with the list ad injinitum-cannot be solved by political partisanship, by destructive criticism
or by political jockeying but only by a patient effort at understanding and by unity of purpose on the part of every Canadian. The same principle applies with greater force to the problems confronting the united nations. If people come there with an axe to grind and without any ideas of co-operation they are bound to defeat the high purpose and ideals of the united nations.
